messages.subject: intercept as grand mean in logistic regressions and new question
messages.subject_clean: intercept as grand mean in logistic regressions and new question
messages.body_plain:
Hello  

Thank you very much for your answers, Dale, Titus and Dan!
Titus answered my question fully, I re-worked your R code on my
computer, and I am satisfied that, in a regression _without_ random
effects, the intercept is not the ordinary grand mean that I naively
thought it was (logit of 768 / 1068) , but the mean of the logit means
of the different levels of a variable. 

Regarding Dale's answer, I just
to make sure I understand properly, because I am a bit confused: In your
answer you are mainly talking about why we cannot expect certain things
to correspond in a model _with_ random effects - did I understand
correctly? However, my original question was about why certain things
did not correspond in a model _without_ random effects.  

Now I have
another question. I have read that it is a problem (see especially
Florian Jaeger's blog) when our data is not fully balanced, i.e. when we
do not have the same number of cases per condition, and so far I have
addressed the imbalance by centering/scaling variables with 2 levels
with "scale as numeric" and using the centered variables as predictors.


If INSTEAD of centering predictors with "scale as numeric" we use sum
coding contrasts (i.e. contrasts(data$variable)  There's also a simpler
reason why the grand mean doesn't equal the intercept, even without
random effects.
> 
> Say you have one predictor with levels A and B,
that will always come out as and -X in sum contrasts with the intercept
bang in the middle.
> 
> But if A has more observations than B or vice
versa, the grand mean will not be equal to the intercept. It will be
skewed by the token numbers, in a way that the intercept (and other
coefficients) never are.
> 
> Is it not so?
> Dan
> 
>> On 25 Sep 2015,
at 12:29, Dale Barr wrote: What Titus said is correct. The only time the
intercept will correspond to the grand mean in a generalized linear
model is when you are using the identity link. Basically what is going
on in a logit model is the model assumes that random intercepts are
normally distributed around the intercept on the *logit* scale. So your
intercept is the "conditional" estimate of the grand mean (in that it is
conditional on a random effect of zero). This can differ from the
"marginal" mean (the mean *ignoring* the distribution of your random
effects). Indeed, the further away the intercept is from zero in log
odds space, the more the conditional and marginal means will diverge,
due to the projection from log odds to probability space. The divergence
doesn't mean there there is anything wrong with your analysis; they are
just different ways of looking at the same data. If you want to do your
analysis on the marginal values, you would need to use a different
approach: Generalized Estimation Equations. You can read about
"subject-specific" vs. "population average models" in Raudenbush & Bryk,
Hierarchical Linear Models. I think there is also some discussion in a
textbook on longitudinal data analysis by Fitzmaurice, Laird, and Ware.

>>

central point is that the mean of the logit of two values (condition
means) is not the same as the logit of the mean of those values. #
